newsitem.title: TURKEY: Israel and Turkish Islamists agree to disagree.
newsitem.headline: Israel and Turkish Islamists agree to disagree.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists have agreed to disagree with Israel on the stalled Middle East peace process and focus on developing economic ties, Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said on Wednesday.
Levy told journalists he and Turkey's Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, had warmed to each other at a meeting on Tuesday night after some contentious moments.

"Of course we might not have agreed on all issues. No one should expect the other side to accept all their views but there is a desire on both sides to develop and strengthen relations," he said after a lunch with Turkish business leaders.

Erbakan gave Levy a pro-Palestinian reprimand in front of the television cameras before their talks. He told the Jewish state to abandon its claim to the whole of Jerusalem and hand occupied land over to the Arabs.
"Above all (Israel) must always recognise that Jerusalem is a sacred city for all peoples...for Moslems as well as for Christians and Jews," Erbakan said.
Levy said he was not put off by Erbakan's comments.
"I am trying to convince him, he is trying to convince me. We have reached an agreement in principle to expand economic relations," said Levy.
Erbakan promised in 1995 election campaigning to "liberate" Jerusalem, which Israel sees as its eternal and united capital, but the realities of office have forced him to tone down his rhetoric.
Turkey's influential military has put an end to Islamist talk of scrapping a military deal under which Israeli air force jets have trained in Turkish skies.
And parliament last week passed an economic agreement with Israel under which trade is expected to quadruple to $2 billion by the year 2000.
Erbakan aides, however, said no punches were pulled when it came to Middle East peace.
"Both sides, both Erbakan and Levy, made it very clear. They made their points, or at least both sides understood each other directly," State Minister Abdullah Gul told Reuters in Ankara.

Anatolian news agency quoted Oguzhan Asilturk, a leading member of Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party as saying Erbakan had also demanded that Israel end building Jewish settlements in east Jerusalem and abide by peace accords with the Palestinians.
"Turkey cannot be too close to Israel at a time when the whole Moslem world and the Arab countries are boycotting Israel," Asilturk said.
Arab nations have threatened to freeze relations with Israel and reintroduce an economic boycott in frustration at what they see as Israeli delays in the peace process.

Israeli troops shot and wounded 31 Palestinians with rubber bullets on Wednesday in Hebron in the latest clashes since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent bulldozers to start a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
An attempt to revive the peace process by U.S. President Bill Clinton has failed to halt the violence.
